subject: Pathology
summary: Prefrontal association area pathology often presents as executive dysfunction, impaired planning, and disinhibition. It is usually secondary to vascular, infectious, or degenerative insults. Early recognition guides targeted therapy and prevents complications.

sections.p: Damage to the prefrontal association cortex, especially the dorsolateral region, disrupts executive functions. Diagnosis combines clinical assessment with neuroimaging when available.

t.b: Lesion in DLPC confirms focal damage

sections.p: Severity is graded by functional impact: mild (occasional lapses), moderate (daily impairment), severe (inability to perform ADLs).
In low‑resource settings, vascular insults and infections dominate.
Patients exhibit impaired planning, poor judgment, and emotional lability. They may also have memory deficits and slowed thought processes.
Use available tools to confirm etiology and rule out mimics.
b: Blood tests: CBC, ESR, HIV, TB markers

t.b: Elevated suggests infectious or inflammatory cause

sections.p: Urgent signs include sudden worsening, seizures, or focal deficits indicating hemorrhage or infection progression.
Treat underlying cause, provide supportive care, and monitor for complications. Pharmacologic choices aim to improve cognition and prevent side effects.
Regular neuropsychological assessment, blood pressure control, infection screening, and rehabilitation improve outcomes.
Other causes of executive dysfunction can mimic prefrontal lesions.
Normal imaging does not exclude functional deficits; low-grade infections may show subtle changes.
b: CT may miss small ischemic lesions
EEG can be normal in chronic injury

faq.a: Early treatment of reversible causes like infection or stroke can restore function, but permanent damage often remains.

faq.q: What is the most common cause in low‑resource settings?
faq.a: Stroke, especially hemorrhagic, and infectious meningitis are frequent.
They may control agitation but do not treat underlying pathology and can worsen cognition.

exam: Explain how a stroke in the dorsolateral prefrontal cortex leads to impaired planning and disinhibition.
Describe the diagnostic workup for a patient with new executive dysfunction in a low‑resource hospital.
Outline the management steps for a patient with suspected tuberculous meningitis affecting the prefrontal cortex.
